topicName: EIPs & Hard Forks: Cancun, EIP-1559, EIP-4844 (Blobs)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"EIPs & Hard Forks: Cancun, EIP-1559, and EIP-4844 (Blobs)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Ethereum evolves through Ethereum Improvement Proposals (EIPs) and coordinated network upgrades known as Hard Forks. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for Web3 developers building scalable and cost-effective decentralized applications."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"What is an EIP and a Hard Fork?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"An EIP is a design document providing information to the Ethereum community or describing a new feature for Ethereum or its processes. When a group of EIPs are scheduled for implementation together, they form a Hard Fork. A hard fork is a radical change to the protocol that makes previously invalid blocks/transactions valid (or vice-versa), requiring all node operators to upgrade their client software."},{"order":5,"type":"heading","text":"EIP-1559: Fee Market Reform"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"The Mechanics of Transaction Pricing"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"Introduced in the London upgrade, EIP-1559 overhauled the way transaction fees work on Ethereum. Instead of a purely auction-based system where users overpay to ensure inclusion, EIP-1559 introduced a base fee that is burned (removed from circulation) and a priority fee (tip) paid directly to validators."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"// Example transaction structure post EIP-1559 in ethers.js
const tx = {
  to: '0x71C...',
  value: ethers.parseEther('1.0'),
  maxFeePerGas: ethers.parseUnits('50', 'gwei'),
  maxPriorityFeePerGas: ethers.parseUnits('2', 'gwei')
};"},{"order":9,"type":"heading","text":"The Cancun Upgrade (Dencun) & EIP-4844"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Scaling Layer 2 with Blobs"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Cancun-Dencun (Dencun) upgrade went live in early 2024, introducing EIP-4844, also known as Proto-Danksharding. This EIP fundamentally changed how Layer 2 (L2) rollups post data to Ethereum, drastically reducing transaction costs for end users on networks like Arbitrum, Optimism, and Base."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Blobs (Binary Large Objects): Temporary data structures attached to blocks that L2s use to store transaction data cheaply."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Data Expiration: Blob data is pruned after approximately 18 days, preventing permanent state bloat on validator nodes."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Separate Fee Market: Blobs have their own pricing mechanism distinct from standard gas, insulating L1 users from L2 data spikes."},{"order":15,"type":"heading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"By combining the predictable fee burning of EIP-1559 with the massive L2 data scaling capabilities of EIP-4844 in the Cancun upgrade, Ethereum continues its roadmap toward high throughput and sustainable decentralized economics."}]
